questions.question: A savings table has two columns, Week and Money added. Every row is the same: Week 1 adds $5, Week 2 adds $5, Week 3 adds $5, and the table keeps going with $5 in every row. Ben's goal is $45 for a soccer ball. How many rows (weeks) of this table does he need to reach $45?
questions.explain: To plan a savings goal, divide the goal by the amount saved each week: 45 ÷ 5 = 9 weeks. A common trap is subtracting once (45 - 5 = 40) instead of finding how many $5 rows fit inside $45.

questions.question: A savings table lists Week 1 → $6 added, Week 2 → $6 added, Week 3 → $6 added, and so on, with $6 added in every single row. Amara's goal is $27 for a hoodie. How many weeks does she need before she has at least $27?
questions.explain: 27 ÷ 6 = 4 with a remainder of 3, and after 4 weeks she has only $24, so she needs one more week — 5 weeks. The trap is dropping the remainder and answering 4 weeks; part of a week still means a whole extra week of saving.

questions.question: A savings table has a Total saved column: after Week 1 it reads $12, after Week 2 $24, after Week 3 $36, and it keeps growing by $12 each week because Jonah puts in $12 every week. His goal is $80 for a fishing rod. In which week does the Total saved column first reach at least $80?
questions.explain: Keep adding $12: week 6 shows $72, which is still under $80, so week 7 ($84) is the first row that reaches the goal. The trap is stopping at 6 because 80 ÷ 12 = 6 R 8 — the leftover $8 still has to be saved, so round up to 7 weeks.

questions.question: A savings table shows the same amount in every row: $7 added in Week 1, $7 in Week 2, $7 in Week 3, and $7 in every row after that. Priya's goal is $50 for a swim pass. How many weeks does she need before she has at least $50?
questions.explain: 50 ÷ 7 = 7 with a remainder of 1, and 7 weeks gives only $49, so an eighth week is needed. Answering 7 weeks ignores that last $1 — always round the number of weeks up when there is a remainder.

questions.question: A savings goal is $96. The plan is to save $15 every week, starting from $0. How many weeks are needed to reach the goal?
questions.explain: 96 ÷ 15 = 6 R 6, and 6 weeks gives only $90, so the plan needs 7 weeks. Weeks are counted in whole numbers, so a leftover amount always means one more full week, not a part of a week.

questions.question: Leo wants a $150 skateboard. He already has $45 saved and adds $12 to his savings every week. How many more weeks until he can buy the skateboard?
questions.explain: First find the difference he still needs: 150 - 45 = 105, then 105 ÷ 12 = 8 R 9, so 8 weeks gives only $96 more and he needs 9 weeks. Two traps here: forgetting the $45 he already has, and dropping the remainder.

questions.question: Nadia gets $20 income each week from helping at her family's store, and her weekly expense is $12.50 for snacks and bus fare. She puts everything left over into savings for a $50 pair of running shoes. How many weeks until she can buy them?
questions.explain: Savings each week is income minus expense: 20 - 12.50 = $7.50, and 7.50 x 6 = $45 while 7.50 x 7 = $52.50, so she needs 7 weeks. The big trap is planning with the $20 income instead of the $7.50 she actually saves.

questions.question: A savings goal is $40.00. The weekly saving is $4.75. How many whole weeks are needed before there is at least $40.00?
questions.explain: 4.75 x 8 = $38.00, which is short of $40.00, and 4.75 x 9 = $42.75, so 9 weeks are needed. Stopping at 8 weeks because the total is 'close enough' is the same mistake as ignoring a remainder — the goal is not reached until the total is at least $40.00.

questions.question: Sofia wants a $130 bike. She has $34 saved. Each week she earns $20 delivering flyers in her Surrey neighbourhood and spends $9 of it at the pool. She saves the rest. How many weeks until she has enough for the bike?
questions.explain: She saves 20 - 9 = $11 a week and still needs 130 - 34 = $96, so 96 ÷ 11 = 8 R 8; after 8 weeks she has only $88 more, so 9 weeks are needed. Watch two traps: planning with the $20 income instead of the $11 saved, and dropping the remainder to say 8 weeks.

questions.question: Liam's goal is $95 for a camping tent. He saves $14 every week and starts from $0. He works out 95 ÷ 14 = 6 R 11 and tells his family, 'My plan takes 6 weeks.' What should he say instead?
options: He is right — 6 weeks works, because the $11 left over does not really matter.
He needs 7 weeks — after 6 weeks he has only $84, so one more week of saving is required.
He should say 6 weeks and 11 days, because the remainder tells you the extra days.
He should say 11 weeks, because the remainder in the division is 11.
questions.explain: In a savings plan the remainder means money still missing, so you round the number of weeks up: 6 weeks gives $84, and week 7 brings him to $98, past $95. The remainder 11 is dollars, not weeks and not days.

questions.question: Over the last four weeks Ava saved $9, $12, $8 and $11. She decides her financial plan will use the mean of those four amounts as her weekly saving from now on. Her goal is $75 for concert tickets, starting from $0. How many weeks will her plan take?
questions.explain: The mean is (9 + 12 + 8 + 11) ÷ 4 = 40 ÷ 4 = $10 a week, and 75 ÷ 10 = 7 R 5, so 7 weeks gives only $70 and she needs 8 weeks. The trap is answering 7 and forgetting the last $5 still has to be saved.

questions.question: Noah wants a $180 snowboard before the hill opens in 12 weeks. He already has $20 saved and plans to put away $14 every week. Which statement about his plan is correct?
options: 11 weeks — he reaches the goal with a week to spare.
13 weeks — he misses the opening, because 180 ÷ 14 = 12 R 12.
9 weeks — he makes it early, because 180 ÷ 20 = 9.
12 weeks — he has $188 by the end of week 12, so he just makes it.
questions.explain: He still needs 180 - 20 = $160, and 160 ÷ 14 = 11 R 6, so 11 weeks gives only $174 in total and he needs the full 12 weeks ($20 + $168 = $188). Dropping that remainder makes the plan look a week faster than it really is.
